original_question: Fix integers m >= 2, n >= 2, and j in [n]. Let A be a nonnegative tensor of order m and dimension n, and let M(A) denote its majorization matrix, defined by M(A)_{ij} = a_{ij...j}. Call A j-primitive if there exists a positive integer k such that (M(A^k))_{u j} > 0 for every u in [n], and let γ_j(A) be the least such k. Define R_j(m, n) to be the set of integers k for which there exists a nonnegative tensor A of order m and dimension n that is j-primitive but not primitive, with γ_j(A) = k. Does the set R_j(m, n) have gaps, meaning missing integers between two values that do occur?
target_in_paper: Section 4, Question 4.14: the open problem asking whether the set R_j(m,n) has gaps. In the surrounding Section 4 discussion, this question is posed after introducing the study of j-primitive but non-primitive tensors via the quantities r(m,n) and R_j(m,n), and it relies on the Section 2 definition of j-primitivity and j-primitive degree. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0024379515002244?utm_source=openai))
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the right object and the right level of specificity: it fixes m,n,j; uses the majorization matrix M(A)_{ij}=a_{ij...j}; defines j-primitivity through positivity of the jth column of M(A^k); uses the least such k as gamma_j(A); restricts to tensors that are j-primitive but not primitive; and asks exactly about the existence of gaps in the resulting degree set R_j(m,n). That is essentially the paper’s Section 4 open problem rather than a broader neighboring question. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0024379515002244?utm_source=openai))
missing_details: The ambient coefficient set should be made explicit: a 'nonnegative tensor' here means an order-m, dimension-n tensor with entries in the nonnegative reals. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0024379515002244?utm_source=openai))

To be fully stand-alone, one should say that A^k is the k-th power taken with respect to the general tensor product used throughout the paper; otherwise M(A^k) is not formally defined. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0024379515002244?utm_source=openai))

The paper’s notion of a 'gap' comes from the introduction’s matrix-exponent discussion: a gap is a nonempty consecutive interval of integers missing from the set under study. Your draft paraphrases this informally, but the formal meaning is still implicit. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0024379515002244?utm_source=openai))

If one wants the question to match the paper’s notation as closely as possible, R_j(m,n) should be defined as the set of attained j-primitive degrees gamma_j(A) for nonnegative order-m, dimension-n tensors A that are j-primitive but not primitive; this is what your draft already does, but it is worth stating as a displayed set definition in the final version. refined_question: Fix integers m,n >= 2 and j in [n]:={1,2,...,n}. Let A=(a_{i_1...i_m}) be a nonnegative tensor in R_+^{[m,n]}, and let M(A) be its majorization matrix, defined by M(A)_{ij}=a_{ij...j}. For k >= 1, let A^k denote the k-th power of A with respect to the general tensor product used in the paper. Call A j-primitive if there exists k >= 1 such that (M(A^k))_{uj} > 0 for every u in [n], and let gamma_j(A) be the least such k. Define R_j(m,n):={gamma_j(A) : A is a nonnegative tensor of order m and dimension n that is j-primitive but not primitive}. Must R_j(m,n) be gap-free, or can it contain gaps, i.e. nonempty consecutive intervals of integers none of whose elements belong to R_j(m,n)?
justification: This draft is not aiming at the paper’s introductory upper-bound conjecture; it is aiming at the later open problem in Section 4 about the structure of the set of j-primitive degrees for tensors that are j-primitive but not primitive. The decisive textual match is the paper’s explicit Question 4.14, 'Does there exist gaps in R_j(m,n)?' The nearby context first recalls the Section 2 definitions of j-primitivity and gamma_j(A), then motivates the study of tight bounds for gamma_j(A) in the non-primitive j-primitive case, and then introduces r(m,n) and R_j(m,n) before posing Question 4.14. The only real upgrades needed are to make the tensor-power convention explicit and to formalize 'gap' in the same consecutive-integer sense introduced earlier in the paper. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0024379515002244?utm_source=openai))
